function.name: telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get
function.description: Retrieves specified telemetry information for a network interface within a given fabric, node, and pod, filtered by the interface and information types. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

fabricName.description: The name of the fabric to limit the nodes pertaining to the given fabric name.

nodeId.description: The identifier of the node to limit the results pertaining to the given node ID.

podId.description: The identifier of the pod to limit the results pertaining to the given pod ID.

interfaceType.description: The type of the interface to limit the results pertaining to the given interface type.

infoType.description: The type of information to retrieve about the interface.

message.content:
Below is a quick‑start guide you can follow (or adapt) if you’re looking to pull **all node details** from the *“test‑de”* fabric whose controller/API gateway sits at IP 23.31.32.1.

> ⚠️ These examples assume:
>
> - You already have access credentials (username/password or token).
> - Your device exposes a standard Cisco Telemetry RESTCONF service (`https://{host}/restconf/...`) or a similar HTTP(S)-based telemetry API.
> - TLS certificates are trusted or you’ll add `--insecure` when testing locally.

---

### 1️⃣ Identify the correct API path

For most modern Cisco devices running IOS XE 17.x+ (and many NX‑OS switches), the “nodes” resource lives under the **fabrics** hierarchy:

```
/api/v2/telemetry/fabrics/{fabric-name}/nodes
```

So for your case it would resolve to:

```
https://23.31.32.1/api/v2/telemetry/fabrics/test-de/nodes
```

If you’re working against a legacy platform or a different vendor’s stack, look up their equivalent URI – often it will still contain `/nodes`, `/devices`, or `/inventory`.

---

### 2️⃣ Build the request

#### Using curl

```bash
curl --request GET \
     --url https://23.31.32.1/api/v2/telemetry/fabrics/test-de/nodes \
     --header "Accept: application/json" \
     --basic-auth <USERNAME>:<PASSWORD>   # or replace with Bearer header below
```

Or, if you prefer bearer tokens:

```bash
TOKEN=$(cat ~/.token)
curl --request GET \
     --url https://23.31.32.1/api/v2/telemetry/fabrics/test-de/nodes \
     --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     --header "Accept: application/json"
```

#### Using PowerShell

```powershell
$uri      = "https://23.31.32.1/api/v2/telemetry/fabrics/test-de/nodes"
$username = "<YOUR_USER>"
$password = ConvertTo-SecureString "<YOUR_PASS>" -AsPlainText -Force
$cred     = New-Object System.Management.Automation.PSCredential ($username,$password)

Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $uri `
                  -Credential $cred `
                  -Headers @{ Accept="application/json" } `
                  -UseBasicParsing
```

---

### 3️⃣ What you should see back

A typical JSON payload looks roughly like this:

```json
{
  "nodes": [
    {
      "id": 101,
      "hostname": "leaf01.test-de.corp.local",
      "role": "Leaf",
      "model": "Nexus9000 C9300v",
      "serialNumber": "JAB12345678",
      "softwareVersion": "IOSXE 16.9.5",
      "uptimeSeconds": 86400,
      "lastUpdated": "2026-05-12T14:30:07Z"
    },
    ...
  ]
}
```

Fields may vary depending on the underlying OS version and whether additional telemetry modules are enabled. If you’d rather filter down to certain attributes, check the documentation for supported query options such as `?$filter=` or `$select=`.

---

### 4️⃣ Troubleshooting tips

| Symptom | Likely cause & fix |
|---------|--------------------|
| **401 Unauthorized** | Wrong creds/token → double‑check username/password or refresh token. |
| **404 Not Found** | Fabric name typo OR wrong base URL. Verify that `test-de` exists (`GET /api/v2/telemetry/fabrics`). |
| **500 Internal Server Error** | Backend issue or missing telemetry module. Check logs on the device or contact support. |
| **Connection timed out** | Network reachability problem. Ping 23.31.32.1 first, then ensure port 443/TCP is open. |

---

### 5️⃣ Optional: Pull more granular data per node

Once you’ve identified each node’s unique ID (e.g., `101` above), you can drill into its individual telemetry endpoints:

```
GET https://23.31.32.1/api/v2/telemetry/fabrics/test-de/nodes/<NODE_ID>/interfaces
GET https://23.31.32.1/api/v2/telemetry/fabrics/test-de/nodes/<NODE_ID>/status
...
```

These sub‑resources expose detailed statistics, error counters, and configuration snapshots—useful for troubleshooting or automated monitoring scripts.

---

That’s basically everything you need to fetch the list of nodes belonging to the *“test‑de”* fabric from the host at 23.31.32.1. Once you have the raw JSON, feel free to pipe it through jq, PowerShell's `ConvertFrom-Json`, or whatever tooling fits your workflow!
